newsitem.title: USA: Baby Bells cutting 100 jobs from TELE-TV venture.
newsitem.headline: Baby Bells cutting 100 jobs from TELE-TV venture.

text.p: Former CBS Inc. broadcasting head Howard Stringer resigned Friday as chairman of Tele-TV, the joint television venture formed by three regional Bell telephone companies, which also announced 100 job cuts that will halve Tele-Tv's work force.
Published reports said Stringer, 55, is negotiating for a top position with Sony Corp. of America.

The job cuts over the next several months will fall on Tele-TV operations in New York, Los Angeles, Reston, Va.; and San Ramon, Calif., phone companies Bell Atlantic Corp., Nynex Corp. and Pacific Telesis Group, said in a statement. Some of the employees whose positions are being eliminated will be offered jobs with the Baby Bells, the companies said.
About 100 Tele-TV jobs will remain, Bell Atlantic spokesman Brian Wood. They will be based mainly in Reston and Los Angeles.
"Tele-TV is living but it's slimmed down somewhat," Wood said in a telephone interview. The venture had 270 employees, its peak payroll, last fall, he said..

Analysts said the cuts were inevitable and had been expected because the interactive TV market had not taken off as fast and as sweepingly as had been initially expected. They said the enterprise had been foundering over the past year.
"Everyone's been anticipating that in some fashion Tele-TV would wind down," Credit Suisse First Boston analyst Frank Governali said in an interview.

Tele-TV was formed in 1994 to develop home entertainment, information and interactive services amid hoopla over the prospect of telephone companies moving into a field previously reserved for broadcast and cable TV companies.

One element drawing attention was the 1995 arrival of Stringer, an Oxford University-educated native of Britain known for his skill at corporate politics who left his job as head of CBS broadcasting. Stringer was a 22-year veteran of the "Tiffany network" whose career there included heading CBS News.
The departure of Stringer, who was also Tele-TV's chief executive, leaves Chief Operating Officer David Grant in charge of Tele-TV media and President Ed Grebow heading Tele-TV Systems.
The cuts announced Friday will enable Tele-TV to support the individual video strategies of its owners in a more cost-effective way, the phone companies said.
"There's not enough common thread to our video strategies to support such a large Tele-TV operation," Wood said.

He explained that, while Pacific Telesis was delivering video over coaxial cable in San Jose, Calif., and developing a wireless cable TV system in Los Angeles, Bell Atlantic and Nynex were looking to use fiber optic cable to provide video and communications services.
Bell Atlantic is building such a system in Philadelphia and expects to offer telephone service by the end of this year and video in 1998, Wood said.
Tele-TV will handle deals with television programmers for content and technology vendors for the three Bells, he said.

Gary Arlen, president of Arlen Communications of Bethesda, Md., which watches the industry, said a key obstacle to interactive TV and video-on-demand is resistence among its target audience -- consumers 40 and older, who would rather be couch potatoes when watching TV.
The industry may eventually take off as younger consumers come of age, he said. In the interim, Tele-TV has struggled, he said.
"Tele-TV is a company that has been searching for a mission for the past six months," said Arlen.
